questions.text: 1.1. Perform a SWOT (strength, weakness, opportunities and threats) analysis of the project. (4 x 4 = 16)
questions.correctAnswer: Strengths: planned accessible capsules at major retail entrances; partnerships with business and government; clear environmental purpose and potential recovery of valuable materials; awareness and safe disposal goals. Weaknesses: the earlier workshop approach had low user uptake; users may still avoid making an effort; capsule placement, collection and maintenance/logistics require coordination; contamination or incorrect disposal may affect operations. Opportunities: expand collection points through retailers and municipalities; public-awareness campaigns and incentives; build a circular-economy/reuse market for recovered materials; use participation data to improve locations and service. Threats: users continue storing devices or putting them in ordinary waste; vandalism, theft or hazardous contamination; costs or partner permissions delay deployment; other recyclers or weak resale demand reduce revenue.
aiRubric: Strengths: up to 4 distinct, case-linked points (4).
Weaknesses: up to 4 distinct, case-linked points (4).
Opportunities: up to 4 distinct, case-linked points (4).
Threats: up to 4 distinct, plausible points (4).
questions.aiReferenceNotes: Mark with the method shown in the key, while accepting equivalent valid wording, workings, units and sensible rounding. The reference answer is a study aid, not an official memorandum.
questions.explanation:
SWOT separates internal strengths and weaknesses from external opportunities and threats. Strong responses apply each category to E-GREEN, the earlier low-uptake experience and the new retail capsule plan.

Student note: Do not place a future market opportunity under strengths or an external threat under weaknesses.
questions.studentNote: Do not place a future market opportunity under strengths or an external threat under weaknesses.

questions.text: 3.1. Illustrate the mobile app design activities listed in Table 3 in an activity-on-arrow (AoA) diagram. Adopt the layout illustrated in Figure 1. (16)
questions.correctAnswer: One valid AOA structure: 1→2 A(3); 2→3 B(3); 2→4 C(5); 2→5 D(4); 3→6 E(1); 4→7 F(2); 5→8 G(5); 6→9 dummy; 7→9 dummy; 8→9 dummy; 9→10 H(1). Earliest event times: 1=0, 2=3, 3=6, 4=8, 5=7, 6=7, 7=10, 8=12, 9=12, 10=13. Latest event times: 1=0, 2=3, 3=11, 4=10, 5=7, 6=12, 7=12, 8=12, 9=12, 10=13. Other valid event numbering and dummy-arrow layouts are acceptable if dependencies are preserved.
aiRubric: Represent all eight activities with correct durations and precedence (7).
Use valid AOA merge logic for H’s three predecessors, with dummy arrows if required (3).
Correct backward-pass event times and start/finish nodes (2).
Diagram legible with event numbers, labels and durations (2).
questions.aiReferenceNotes: Mark with the method shown in the key, while accepting equivalent valid wording, workings, units and sensible rounding. The reference answer is a study aid, not an official memorandum.
questions.explanation:
H can begin only when E, F and G are all complete. The longest path is A–D–G–H at 13 days; dummy arrows preserve the three incoming dependencies without adding time.

Student note: AOA places activities on arrows and events at nodes. AON places activities in nodes, so do not reverse the requested notation.
questions.studentNote: AOA places activities on arrows and events at nodes. AON places activities in nodes, so do not reverse the requested notation.
